The UAE says Iran attacked another ADNOC vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, marking the third such incident in less than a week.

No injuries were reported.

Abu Dhabi urged Tehran to halt the attacks and fully reopen Hormuz, while warning it will defend its navigation rights and national interests.

Trump meanwhile told Americans that higher gasoline prices are a necessary cost of confronting Iran, as U.S. pump prices stand 29% above year-ago levels.

JANE STREET TAKES $15 BILLION JULY HIT

Jane Street lost about $15 billion in July as the AI selloff hit its exposure to Situational Awareness and other technology positions, Reuters reports.

The firm has still generated more than $40 billion in trading revenue this year.

Following the losses, Jane Street told employees it had significantly reduced risk in affected strategies and would become more selective.

IRAN REJECTS TRUMP’S HORMUZ THREAT

Iran says it will not be intimidated after President Trump threatened to declare the Strait of Hormuz U.S. territory.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said decisions over opening or closing the strategic waterway remain solely under Iran’s authority.

The comments signal continued confrontation over control of the critical global energy route.

Countries aligned with the U.S.-led Pax Silica framework could risk exclusion if they also participate in Beijing’s coalition.

The strategy aims to secure AI chips, models and critical-mineral supply chains as Chinese open-weight models gain ground against U.S. rivals.

Ed Yardeni raised his S&P 500 target to 8,400 from 8,250, citing “fabulous earnings momentum.”

He now expects 2026 S&P 500 earnings of $375, up from $330, as companies broadly beat forecasts.

Yardeni sees the earnings-driven rally continuing and maintains his 10,000 target for 2029.

CPI EASES PRESSURE ON FED TO HIKE

July CPI came in close enough to expectations to reduce pressure on the Fed to raise rates in September, according to Nick Timiraos.

The Fed has argued current rates are restrictive enough to bring inflation toward 2% without further hikes.

But persistent tariffs, energy pressures and AI-driven demand for technology equipment and software are complicating that outlook.

For now, the CPI report gives policymakers more room to hold rates steady.

WHEAT JUMPS AFTER RUSSIAN PORT STRIKE

Wheat futures surged 2.4% after Ukrainian drones reportedly struck two grain terminals at Russia’s Novorossiysk port.

The terminals handle roughly 15 million metric tons of grain exports annually, raising concerns over disruptions to Russian wheat shipments.

The extent of the damage remains unclear, but analysts warn Russia could struggle to maintain normal export volumes.

Corn rose 0.6%, while soybeans gained 0.3%.

Norway’s sovereign wealth fund posted a record $185 billion first-half profit, delivering a 12.95% return as semiconductor stocks surged.

But CEO Nicolai Tangen warned investors not to expect similar returns ahead, citing geopolitical tensions, inflation and potential market weakness.

His advice: stay invested, think long term and remain diversified.

Tangen expects tougher markets ahead after years of exceptionally strong returns.

BURRY: BERKSHIRE HAS LOST ITS BUFFETT EDGE

Michael Burry says Berkshire Hathaway is no longer attractive under CEO Greg Abel, questioning his capital-allocation discipline.

Others disagree, arguing Abel remains disciplined and Berkshire’s strong balance sheet, earnings growth and cash deployment continue to support the investment case.

IRAN DENIES CEASEFIRE EXTENSION TALKS

Iran says there have been no talks to extend a 60-day ceasefire with the U.S., rejecting reports that an agreement had been reached.

A senior Iranian source told Reuters that discussions via mediators instead focus on Washington returning to the interim pact and setting a timeline for its commitments.

Iran says no progress has been made, accusing the U.S. of violating the agreement shortly after it was signed.

The Strait of Hormuz remains a key sticking point.

HORMUZ TRAFFIC REMAINS NEAR A STANDSTILL

Only 14 vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, according to Kpler, despite Trump declaring the waterway “open.”

That remains far below the roughly 120 vessels per day seen before the war.

Of those 14 ships, 11 used the Iranian-approved route, while none used the traditional central passage.

Kpler says the modest traffic increase does not signal normalization, keeping pressure on global oil supplies.

SEPTEMBER FED HIKE LOOKS UNLIKELY

Baird’s Ross Mayfield says softer core inflation and limited wage pressure strengthen the case for the Fed to hold rates steady in September.

He sees those trends as the “bedrock” for a pause, reducing the likelihood of another rate hike at the next meeting.

ENERGY COULD REIGNITE INFLATION IN AUGUST

Falling energy prices helped cool July inflation, with gasoline down 2.9% M/M and fuel oil falling 1.7%.

But that relief may be temporary.

Rising crude prices and strong refining margins are already pushing fuel costs higher.

U.S. gasoline now averages $4.03 per gallon, up from $3.87 a month ago, suggesting energy could put renewed upward pressure on August inflation.

GOLDMAN: JULY CPI SUPPORTS SEPTEMBER HOLD

Goldman Sachs Asset Management called July CPI “encouraging,” saying contained core inflation strengthens the case for the Fed to hold rates steady in September.

Lindsay Rosner said the report adds to signs that underlying inflation is moderating.

However, another inflation report is due before the September FOMC meeting, meaning the outlook could still shift.

For now, the in-line CPI print supports a Fed pause.
